BDRIBS(1): Poisson model with the total exposure time

Source: vignettes/bdribs1.Rmd
bdribs1.Rmd
library(bssd)

Model

BDRIBS (Bayesian Detection of potential Risk using Inference on Blinded Safety data) is the model of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018). Duncan (2026, Section 3.2.2) calls it BDRIBS(1) when the exposure is the total exposure time of the blinded population. The number of subjects with the event in the blinded data, \(Y\), follows \[Y \sim \mathrm{Poisson}\{E \delta (r k + 1) / (k + 1)\},\] where \(E\) is the total exposure time, \(\delta\) is the event rate on placebo, \(r\) is the rate ratio of the study drug to placebo, and the study drug and placebo are randomized in the ratio \(k:1\). The priors are \[\delta \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\lambda_{HP} PT_{HP} / DF, PT_{HP} / DF), \quad r = \frac{p}{k (1 - p)}, \quad p \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a, b),\] where the Gamma distribution has the shape and rate parameters, \(\lambda_{HP}\) and \(PT_{HP}\) are the event rate and the total patient time of historical placebo data, and \(DF\) is a discount factor for the historical data. The parameter \(p\) is the probability that an event in the blinded data occurred on the study drug. A signal is declared when \(P(r > \theta_c \mid Y) > P_{\mathrm{cutoff}}\).

The arguments of bdribs_post() correspond to the symbols as follows.

Symbol Argument Description
\(Y\) y number of subjects with the event
\(E\) exposure total exposure time, the sum of the follow-up times
\(k\) k randomization ratio of study drug to placebo
\(\lambda_{HP}\) lambda_hp event rate in the historical placebo data
\(PT_{HP}\) pt_hp total patient time of the historical placebo data; Inf fixes \(\delta\) at lambda_hp
\(DF\) df discount factor
\((a, b)\) p_prior shape parameters of the Beta prior of \(p\) (default c(0.5, 0.5))
\(\theta_c\) rr0 critical value of \(r\) (default 1)
\(P_{\mathrm{cutoff}}\) cutoff posterior probability threshold (default 0.95)

The exposure, lambda_hp, pt_hp and the optional time t_star for the cumulative incidences must be in the same time unit.

Example: hypothetical example 2 of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018)

In Section 4.4 of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018), the study drug and placebo are randomized 2:1, the blinded data have 540 patient-years of exposure, and the background rate on placebo is about 0.011 per patient-year, estimated from 33 events in about 3000 patient-years of historical data.

Screening analysis

The screening analysis treats the background rate as known (pt_hp = Inf) and uses the uniform prior for \(p\). Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018, Sections 3.4 and 4.4) compare the posterior probability with the boundary \(3 / (3 + k \theta_c)\), which is used here as cutoff.

screen <- expand.grid(rr0 = c(1, 1.3), y = c(8, 9))
screen$cutoff <- 3 / (3 + 2 * screen$rr0)
screen$prob <- mapply(function(y, rr0, cutoff) {
  bdribs_post(y = y, exposure = 540, k = 2, lambda_hp = 0.011, pt_hp = Inf,
              p_prior = c(1, 1), rr0 = rr0, cutoff = cutoff,
              details = FALSE)$prob
}, screen$y, screen$rr0, screen$cutoff)
screen$signal <- screen$prob > screen$cutoff
Events rr0 Boundary bssd Signal Mukhopadhyay et al.
8 1.0 0.600 0.619 TRUE 0.622
8 1.3 0.536 0.433 FALSE 0.434
9 1.0 0.600 0.753 TRUE 0.756
9 1.3 0.536 0.580 TRUE 0.584

The published values were computed by MCMC with the bdribs package, and they differ from the values of bssd by at most 0.004. With 9 events, the posterior is

fit9 <- bdribs_post(y = 9, exposure = 540, k = 2, lambda_hp = 0.011,
                    pt_hp = Inf, p_prior = c(1, 1))
fit9
#> Model: BDRIBS 
#> Relative risk: rate ratio r of study drug to placebo
#> P(r > 1 | data) = 0.753
#> Signal (posterior probability > 0.95): no
#> Posterior of r: mean 1.522, median 1.438, 95% interval (0.379, 3.143)

Sensitivity analysis

In the second step, the screening analysis is repeated with background rates at the limits of the 90% credible interval of the background rate. As in Section 4.3 of the article, the interval is computed from the Gamma distribution with the number of historical events plus 0.5 as the shape and the historical patient-years plus 0.5 as the rate.

rate_ci <- qgamma(c(0.05, 0.95), shape = 33 + 0.5, rate = 3000 + 0.5)
rate_ci
#> [1] 0.008192346 0.014515593
sens <- expand.grid(rr0 = c(1, 1.3), lambda_hp = rate_ci)
sens$prob <- mapply(function(lambda_hp, rr0) {
  bdribs_post(y = 9, exposure = 540, k = 2, lambda_hp = lambda_hp,
              pt_hp = Inf, p_prior = c(1, 1), rr0 = rr0,
              details = FALSE)$prob
}, sens$lambda_hp, sens$rr0)
Background rate rr0 bssd Mukhopadhyay et al.
0.0082 1.0 0.920 0.92
0.0082 1.3 0.833 0.83
0.0145 1.0 0.478 0.48
0.0145 1.3 0.280 0.28

The interval (0.0082, 0.0145) agrees with the interval (0.0082, 0.0145) of Section 4.4 of the article. The posterior probabilities differ from the published values, which are given to two decimal places, by at most 0.003.

Instead of fixing the background rate, the historical data can be used as the Gamma prior of \(\delta\), which gives the posterior probability unconditional on the background rate (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2018, Section 4.3):

fit_gamma <- bdribs_post(y = 9, exposure = 540, k = 2,
                         lambda_hp = (33 + 0.5) / (3000 + 0.5),
                         pt_hp = 3000 + 0.5, df = 1, p_prior = c(1, 1))
fit_gamma
#> Model: BDRIBS 
#> Relative risk: rate ratio r of study drug to placebo
#> P(r > 1 | data) = 0.7076
#> Signal (posterior probability > 0.95): no
#> Posterior of r: mean 1.494, median 1.373, 95% interval (0.3078, 3.371)

Total exposure time from subject-level data

For subject-level data, time_at_risk() returns the total exposure time (exposure), which BDRIBS(1) uses, and the total time at risk, which BDRIBS(2) uses (vignette("bdribs2")).

time_at_risk(follow_up = c(52, 52, 30, 12), event = c(1, 0, 1, 0),
             event_time = c(10, NA, 25, NA))
#>     exposure time_at_risk      n_event 
#>          146           99            2

Numerical integration

Because the Gamma prior of \(\delta\) is conjugate to the Poisson likelihood, bdribs_post() integrates \(\delta\) out analytically. The remaining posterior quantities are one-dimensional integrals over \(\mathrm{logit}(p)\), which are computed by adaptive quadrature (stats::integrate()) with a relative tolerance of \(10^{-10}\) (see ?bdribs_post). The expected values of the tests in tests/testthat were computed beforehand by independent Python implementations (inst/validation/python/ref_bdribs.py and ref_bdribs_fixed.py).

Comparison with MCMC

The bdribs package of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018) samples the same model by MCMC with JAGS. The script inst/validation/validate_bdribs_package.R compares bdribs_post() with bdribs::bdribs() for the settings below. The results in this section are read from the output of that script (validate_bdribs_package.csv in the folder validation/results of the installed package); JAGS is not run when this article is built.

Data y E k Historical events Historical patient-years Background rate Prior of p
B1 5 500 2 18 4000 fixed (inf.type = 1) Beta(1, 1)
B2 5 500 2 18 4000 Gamma prior (inf.type = 2) Beta(1, 1)
B3 5 500 2 18 4000 fixed (inf.type = 1) Beta(0.5, 0.5)
B4 9 540 2 33 3000 fixed (inf.type = 1) Beta(1, 1)
B5 9 540 2 33 3000 Gamma prior (inf.type = 2) Beta(1, 1)
B6 7 800 1 18 4000 Gamma prior (inf.type = 2) Beta(1, 1)
B7 30 2000 1 20 2000 Gamma prior (inf.type = 2) Beta(0.5, 0.5)

With inf.type = 1, bdribs::bdribs() fixes the background rate at the historical events divided by the historical patient-years, which is bdribs_post() with pt_hp = Inf. With inf.type = 2, it uses the Gamma prior with the shape (historical events + 0.001) and the rate (historical patient-years + 0.001), which is bdribs_post() with these values as lambda_hp * pt_hp and pt_hp and df = 1. bdribs::bdribs() was run with 2 chains, 5,000 burn-in iterations and 100,000 iterations (the arguments nc, burn and iter of mc.params). The Monte Carlo standard error (SE) of each MCMC estimate uses the effective sample size of the draws (coda::effectiveSize()); for the posterior probabilities, the effective sample sizes are between 46,649 and 115,901. For the median, the table shows the MCMC proportion of draws below the posterior median computed by bssd, which should be 0.5. The column Ratio is the absolute difference divided by the SE.

In all 35 items, the bssd value is within 2.6 standard errors of the MCMC value, and 33 items are within two standard errors. The largest absolute difference in a posterior probability is 0.0036, while the SEs of the MCMC probabilities are between 0.0015 and 0.0023. Differences of this size are expected from the Monte Carlo error of MCMC alone, so the difference between the numerical integration of bssd and MCMC is negligible in practice. The validation script judges an item PASS when the difference is at most four standard errors; 35 of the 35 items are PASS.

References

Duncan, B. (2026). Robust safety monitoring and signal detection using alternatives to the standard Poisson distribution. Journal of Biopharmaceutical Statistics, 36(2), 227-244. https://doi.org/10.1080/10543406.2024.2395532

Mukhopadhyay, S., Waterhouse, B., and Hartford, A. (2018). Bayesian detection of potential risk using inference on blinded safety data. Pharmaceutical Statistics, 17(6), 823-834. https://doi.org/10.1002/pst.1898
